title: Constant price of stability for undirected network design
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Is the price of stability of undirected equal-cost-sharing network design games bounded by a universal constant?
definitions: An instance is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative real edge costs c_e and k≥1 players, each with connected terminal pair (s_i,t_i). Player i chooses a simple s_i-to-t_i path (the empty path is allowed if its terminals coincide). For path profile P, let n_e be the number of chosen paths using e. Player i pays ∑_{e∈P_i} c_e/n_e. A pure Nash equilibrium is a profile at which no single player can reduce its own payment by switching to any other feasible path, with the shares recomputed after the deviation. Social cost C(P)=∑_{e:n_e>0}c_e counts every used edge once. OPT is the minimum social cost over all path profiles, equivalently the minimum-cost subgraph connecting all terminal pairs. The assertion is ∃C<∞ such that every instance has a pure Nash profile P with C(P)≤C OPT. This inequality includes OPT=0. It does not require every equilibrium to be cheap or an efficient algorithm for finding one; terminal pairs need not share a common source.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation for the stated model. A bound growing with k or a theorem restricted to common-source instances is insufficient.
context: The original fair-cost-allocation analysis establishes logarithmic dependence on the number of players. A constant independent of that number is the stronger undirected target.
why: The price of stability asks how much inefficiency is unavoidable even in the best stable outcome.

import_provenance.original_title: Constant price of stability for undirected network design
import_provenance.original_statement: In an undirected graph, each player chooses a path between its own terminal pair and each used edge’s cost is split equally among its users. Must there always be a pure Nash equilibrium whose total purchased-edge cost is at most a universal constant times the minimum feasible network cost?
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: The question allows arbitrary terminal pairs; constant bounds for broadcast or other single-source special cases do not settle it.

context_blocks.text: The original fair-cost-allocation analysis establishes logarithmic dependence on the number of players. A constant independent of that number is the stronger undirected target.

sentences: Each player chooses a path joining its own pair of terminals.
Users of an edge split that edge’s cost equally.
A stable profile permits no profitable unilateral path change.
The comparison uses the cheapest stable profile and the socially cheapest network.
The proposed constant must work for arbitrary terminal pairs and player counts.
